explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. He says, "I am He; I am the first, and I am the last." (Isaiah 48:12) That's how He introduces Himself to Jacob and Israel, whom He has called. He tells them who He is before anything else.

explanations.answer: A god of the high hills
explanations.explanation: I see why that one looks tempting, baker, but the text never says it. The LORD says, "I am He; I am the first, and I am the last." (Isaiah 48:12) No hills, no height, no mountain address. He just says who He is, and He starts with the very first and the very last.

Not quite, friend. He says, "I am He; I am the first, and I am the last." (Isaiah 48:12) You can't be the first and the last and also fit in a lineup. Right after this, He asks which of the idols has foretold these things (Isaiah 48:14), and I think that tells you how He sees the lineup.

Yes, baker. The verse says, "when I summon them, they stand up together." (Isaiah 48:13). That's the same hand that founded the earth and spread out the heavens, and now they answer it as one. No late ones, no stragglers, and no one hitting snooze. This is the same One who says, "I am the first, and I am the last." (Isaiah 48:12).

That's a rough picture, friend, and it isn't in the verse. The text says, "when I summon them, they stand up together." (Isaiah 48:13) Standing up is what the earth and the heavens do when He summons them. Picture a whole crowd getting to their feet at the same moment.

Nope, nobody's ducking behind the couch here. The verse says, "when I summon them, they stand up together." (Isaiah 48:13) When He calls, they stand up. I think I'd have tried to hide, but I'm no heaven.

Close, baker, but this one is False. The LORD asks, "Which of the idols has foretold these things?" (Isaiah 48:14) It's a question, and the verse doesn't name a single idol that did. In the next verse He says, "I, even I, have spoken…" (Isaiah 48:15)

That's right, baker. The LORD asks, "Which of the idols has foretold these things?" (Isaiah 48:14) The verse doesn't name any idol that did. Then in the next verse He says, "I, even I, have spoken…" (Isaiah 48:15)

That's it, baker. "The LORD’s chosen ally will carry out His desire against Babylon, and His arm will be against the Chaldeans." (Isaiah 48:14) The Chaldeans are mentioned right alongside it. Both names will come back when we hit verse 20.

Nineveh is a good guess, friend, but it isn't in this verse. The text says the chosen ally will act "…against Babylon, and His arm will be against the Chaldeans." (Isaiah 48:14) Babylon is the name to hold onto here. It comes back in verse 20.

Damascus isn't named here, baker. The text says the LORD's chosen ally will carry out His desire "…against Babylon, and His arm will be against the Chaldeans." (Isaiah 48:14) When you're stuck, the verse itself is the best map I know.

Yes, baker. "I have brought him, and he will succeed in his mission." (Isaiah 48:15). The LORD says this about His chosen ally from the verse before, the one who will carry out His desire against Babylon. He says it plainly, with no maybe in it. Right before that He says, "I, even I, have spoken; yes, I have called him." (Isaiah 48:15).
I know, friend, it sounds like how my Monday goes. But the verse says, "I have brought him, and he will succeed in his mission." (Isaiah 48:15) No struggling is mentioned here. Only success.

Not this time, baker. The LORD says, "I have brought him, and he will succeed in his mission." (Isaiah 48:15) The verse tells us the result, and the result is success. How the ally feels at the door isn't mentioned.
Good thought, baker, but it's False. The LORD says, "From the beginning I have not spoken in secret…" (Isaiah 48:16) He has spoken in the open from the beginning. The verse says it straight out.
That's right, baker. "From the beginning I have not spoken in secret…" (Isaiah 48:16) He says it plainly, in the open. Nothing is hidden in the back of a drawer.

Yes, baker. "And now the Lord GOD has sent me, accompanied by His Spirit." (Isaiah 48:16) The verse doesn't tell us who this speaker is, and I won't guess. What it does say is clear: the Lord GOD sent him, and His Spirit comes along. The sender is named right there in the verse.

I see where that could come from, friend, but the verse names someone else. The speaker says, "…the Lord GOD has sent me, accompanied by His Spirit." (Isaiah 48:16) The sender is the Lord GOD, right there in the text. A king of Babylon isn't mentioned in this passage.

I get why you'd look there, baker, but the elders aren't mentioned in this passage. The speaker says, "…the Lord GOD has sent me, accompanied by His Spirit." (Isaiah 48:16) The sender is right there in the verse. No committee needed.

explanations.answer: Directs them in the way to go
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The LORD says He is the One "…who directs you in the way you should go." (Isaiah 48:17) He teaches and He directs. So He's not only handing out lessons, He's pointing at the road too.

explanations.answer: Lets them pick their own road
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The LORD says He "…directs you in the way you should go." (Isaiah 48:17) He is the One who directs them. Picking their own road isn't what the verse says.

That's not what the verse says, baker. The LORD calls Himself the One "…who directs you in the way you should go." (Isaiah 48:17) He teaches them for their benefit and He directs them. Hiding the way isn't mentioned.

Yes, baker, peace goes in the first blank. "…your peace would have been like a river…" (Isaiah 48:18) A river keeps flowing, and that's the picture He gives for their peace. The waves of the sea come next, for something else.
That's right, baker. "…and your righteousness like waves of the sea." (Isaiah 48:18) Waves keep rolling in and never run out. Two big pictures, one if only.

Nice try, friend, but money never comes up here. The LORD says their peace would have been like a river, "…and your righteousness like waves of the sea." (Isaiah 48:18) Peace and righteousness are what He names.

Good thinking, but a harvest isn't in this verse, baker. The LORD says "…your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like waves of the sea." (Isaiah 48:18) The pictures here are water, not crops.

Not this time, friend. The verse has no armies at all. The LORD says, "…your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like waves of the sea." (Isaiah 48:18) Think of a river that keeps on flowing and waves that keep on rolling in. That's the kind of peace and righteousness He's picturing.

Right, baker. "Your descendants would have been as countless as the sand, and your offspring as numerous as its grains…" (Isaiah 48:19) That's more descendants than I have crumbs on my counter after a big batch. All of it belongs to that same if only. He's describing what could have been.

Careful, friend, this one is True. The LORD says, "Your descendants would have been as countless as the sand…" (Isaiah 48:19) He even adds that their offspring would be as numerous as its grains. That's a whole lot of sand.

Yes, baker. "their name would never be cut off or eliminated from My presence." (Isaiah 48:19) That's part of the same if only, right after the descendants as countless as the sand. Their offspring would be as numerous as its grains, and their name would still stand in His presence. A name that is never cut off is what He pictures.

Good guess, friend, but land isn't in this verse. The LORD says "their name would never be cut off or eliminated from My presence." (Isaiah 48:19). Right before that come the descendants, as countless as the sand and as numerous as its grains. So the verse is about people and their name, not about ground. I think it's a lovely thing to be told, that your name stays in His presence.

Not quite, baker, the temple never comes up in this verse. Look at what the LORD says: "their name would never be cut off or eliminated from My presence." (Isaiah 48:19). Right before it come the descendants, as countless as the sand and as numerous as its grains. So He's talking about people, not buildings. What stays in His presence here is their name.

That's right, baker. "Leave Babylon! Flee from the Chaldeans! Declare it with a shout of joy…" (Isaiah 48:20) The command to leave and the call to declare it come back to back. A shout of joy is what the verse asks for.
Close, friend, but it's True. Right after "Flee from the Chaldeans!" the verse says, "Declare it with a shout of joy…" (Isaiah 48:20) It's a call to be loud about it.

Yes, baker. "The LORD has redeemed His servant Jacob!" (Isaiah 48:20) That's the news the verse says to proclaim with a shout of joy, and to let it go out "…to the ends of the earth…" Good news travels faster than the smell of fresh cookies. Redeemed is the word to hold onto, because the whole shout is built on it.
That's right, baker. "The LORD has redeemed His servant Jacob!" (Isaiah 48:20) Jacob is the name the LORD uses for His people in this passage (Isaiah 48:12). He calls him His servant.

No, friend, that's the opposite of the news. The message is, "The LORD has redeemed His servant Jacob!" (Isaiah 48:20) Redeemed, not forgotten. I know a thing or two about the other word, and this isn't it.
Not this one, baker. The shout going out is, "The LORD has redeemed His servant Jacob!" (Isaiah 48:20) That's the word that fits a shout of joy.

I see why Moses came to mind, friend, but the shout names someone else. It says, "The LORD has redeemed His servant Jacob!" (Isaiah 48:20) Jacob is who the LORD addresses at the start of this passage (Isaiah 48:12). Moses isn't mentioned here.

Not quite, baker, this one is False. The verse says, "They did not thirst when He led them through the deserts…" (Isaiah 48:21) It goes on, "He made water flow for them from the rock; He split the rock, and water gushed out." (Isaiah 48:21) Desert, yes, but water came out of the rock.

That's right, baker. "They did not thirst when He led them through the deserts…" (Isaiah 48:21) The verse goes on, "He made water flow for them from the rock; He split the rock, and water gushed out." (Isaiah 48:21) So the answer is False, because they weren't left thirsty. Desert, yes. Thirst, no.
Yes, baker. "There is no peace…" says the LORD, "for the wicked." (Isaiah 48:22) It's a short line and a heavy one. After a river of peace in verse 18, this is a quiet stop.
No, friend, the poor aren't named here. The LORD says, "There is no peace…" "for the wicked." (Isaiah 48:22) The word is wicked.
I understand the guess, baker, because the weary sure could use peace. But the verse says, "There is no peace…" says the LORD, "for the wicked." (Isaiah 48:22) The weary aren't named there.
